 1                SENATOR KENNEDY:   Thank you, 

 2   Mr. President.  

 3                I rise today to honor a significant 

 4   historical event to Western New York, to Irish 

 5   Americans, to the United States, Canada and 

 6   Ireland -- the Fenian Invasion of 1866 that took 

 7   place on June 1, 1866.  So this week we celebrate 

 8   its 150th anniversary.

 9                Just last week I welcomed to Buffalo 

10   the Lord Mayor of Dublin, Críona Ní Dhálaigh, who 

11   came to our city to help kick off the entire week 

12   of activities honoring this significant event.  

13   This weekend the Consul General of Ireland, 

14   Barbara Jones, will be in town to celebrate the 

15   occasion with us.  The Black Rock Historical 

16   Society, the Ancient Order of Hibernians, and 

17   many different Irish heritage organizations have 

18   come together to put on a magnificent celebration 

19   in honor of this historical occasion.

20                A brief history of the Fenian 

21   Invasion of 1866 will help illustrate the extreme 

22   significance of this anniversary and why such an 

23   event is important to the people of this state 

24   and this country.

25                As I mentioned, on June 1, 1866, 


                                                                3007

 1   about 500 to 800 Irish nationalists and United 

 2   States Civil War veterans, known as Fenians, 

 3   embarked from the docks of the Pratt Ironworks in 

 4   Buffalo to invade Canada, seize it and barter it 

 5   for Irish freedom from British rule.  The Fenian 

 6   brotherhood had been founded in 1858 in the 

 7   United States and found its roots in the United 

 8   Irishmen and other Irish Nationalist groups.  

 9                The Fenian forces -- again, mainly 

10   Civil War veterans that served this country 

11   bravely and proudly -- arrived in Buffalo at the 

12   Exchange Street Train Station.  They gathered in 

13   the Old First Ward, the old Irish neighborhood, 

14   and launched their attack from the Pratt 

15   Ironworks, now known as Tow Path Park.

16                The Fenians defeated the Crown 

17   forces across the Niagara River at the Battle of 

18   Ridgeway, outnumbered and outgunned, and briefly 

19   held Fort Erie, but they suffered a setback when 

20   President Andrew Johnson blocked the 

21   reinforcements and sent Generals Grant and Meade 

22   to quell this invasion.  Now, these Civil War 

23   veterans, still dedicated to their 

24   commander-in-chief, followed his orders, came 

25   back onto U.S. soil, and all were pardoned -- 


                                                                3008

 1   although some had lost their lives.

 2                The Fenian Invasion demonstrated 

 3   that independence and democracy are forces that 

 4   no amount of oppression can prevent.  Even 

 5   outnumbered and outgunned, the Fenians valiantly 

 6   battled the British Crown forces in Canada.  

 7                Despite this, the Fenian invasion 

 8   had a profound and lasting impact on the two 

 9   British colonies, Canada and Ireland.  The 

10   momentum for independence grew in Canada and was 

11   achieved one year and one month to the date, on 

12   July 1, 1867, still to this day celebrated as 

13   Canadian Independence Day.  Each year Canada 

14   celebrates the Fenian raid and, given its 

15   supremely vital importance into the incorporation 

16   of Canada as a nation, this event is recognized 

17   across the globe.

18                In Ireland, 50 years later this also 

19   gave great momentum to the uprising on Easter 

20   Monday in 1916.  This year we celebrate its 

21   centennial.

22                In recognition of the significant 

23   event of the Fenian Invasion of Canada, Buffalo 

24   now has a monument in Tow Path Park, where this 

25   invasion set off from on the banks of the 


                                                                3009

 1   Niagara River, dedicated to this moment in 

 2   history, honoring those brave men and women who 

 3   participated in this significant event for Irish 

 4   independence.

 1                I rise to congratulate and to
